title: The prayer again (Matthew 6:9–15)
hookLine: the Lord's Prayer, set here in the middle of the sermon

lines: BACK AT THE START OF THE PATH.
IN THE MIDDLE OF THE SERMON.
cards: A prayer you know by heart can slip right past you, like the words of a song you've sung a thousand times. Our Father. Hallowed be thy name.
Thy kingdom come. You walked through it one line at a time back in the first weeks of this path, and you might know it by heart now.
Today it turns up in a new place: not on its own, but set right in the middle of the Sermon on the Mount. Where it sits changes how it sounds.

teach.b: Jesus has just said: don't pray to be seen, and don't babble.
Then, in the King James Bible: "After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven."
After this manner: a pattern as well as a script. Short, plain, private enough to say behind a closed door, and yet it says our, not my.

teach.h: AT THE CENTER OF THE SERMON.
teach.b: Many scholars notice that it sits near the very center of the sermon, as if the whole teaching turns around it.
Everything before it, the Beatitudes, reconciling, loving enemies, is what it looks like when thy will be done on earth.

teach.h: PATER NOSTER: BEADS, A ROW, AN ELEVATOR.
teach.b: For centuries, Western Christians prayed it in Latin, and its first two words, Pater noster, our Father, became a word of their own. Medieval prayer beads were called paternosters.
A street near Saint Paul's Cathedral in London is still called Paternoster Row.
There's even an open elevator, a chain of little rooms that never stops moving, called a paternoster, because it goes round and round like beads in praying hands.

teach.h: FORGIVE, AND FOR THINE IS THE KINGDOM.
teach.b: At the end, Matthew adds a line about forgiveness: "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." It's the only line of the prayer Jesus explains.
And the ending many people know, for thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory?

teach.h: THY WILL BE DONE IN EARTH, AS IT IS IN HEAVEN.
teach.b: It's in the King James Bible, but not in the oldest manuscripts of Matthew. It was likely added early for worship.
Protestants usually pray it with the prayer; at Mass, Catholics say it a little later, after the priest's prayer.

how: Christians of every church pray the Lord's Prayer, in worship and at home; many pray it daily, and in most churches the congregation says it together, aloud.

games.q: Jesus has just warned against praying for show and babbling. what does he do next?
o: tells them to pray in silence only.
gives them a short prayer: our Father.
games.why: "After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven." a short prayer, in the middle of the sermon.

practice: If you pray, pray the Lord's Prayer very slowly, one line on each breath: Our Father, which art in heaven; breathe; hallowed be thy name; breathe. Let each line land, and if one catches, stay there.
If you don't pray, listen to the lines in your mind as words people have said for two thousand years, and notice which one stays with you.

wordCard.voice: Paternoster. Latin for our Father: the first words of the Lord's Prayer, which became a name for prayer beads, a London street and an elevator.

orig.note: Latin: our Father. the first words of the Lord's Prayer in the Latin Bible and Mass.

carryVoice: Your line: thy will be done. In earth, as it is in heaven. Two hundred fifty days, a real milestone.
